finding: Obliteration is presented as requiring complete excision and making single-stage graft support impossible. The page's own female series reports two obliterative strictures repaired in one stage with combined dorsal and ventral inlay BMG.
evidence: PMID 41097847, DOI 10.1002/nau.70161, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41097847/ — Jefferson et al. treated 21 women; two with obliterative strictures required combined dorsal and ventral inlay in the same operation.

edit.old: 1. **Obliterative urethral stricture.** No urethral lumen identifiable; the entire strictured segment must be excised, leaving no native wall for single-stage graft support.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)[[10]](#ref10)</sup>
edit.new: 1. **Obliterative or near-obliterative stricture.** Define the length, residual urethral plate and available vascularized tissue. Jefferson et al. treated two obliterative female strictures in one stage with combined dorsal and ventral BMG inlays; obliteration alone does not establish a need for complete excision or staged repair.<sup>[[9]](#ref9)</sup>

finding: The comparison row calls absence of viable local tissue a reason to choose a staged free graft, directly contradicting this page's statement that staging still requires a viable graft bed. Poor vascularization is a reason to consider vascularized tissue or another strategy.
evidence: EAU Urethral Strictures Guideline 2026, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urethral-strictures/chapter/tissue-transfer — §9.1 says flaps carry their own blood supply, do not rely on recipient vascularity, and gives a Weak recommendation to use flaps when the urethral bed is poorly vascularized; this page's Operative Planning Boundary says waiting does not make an avascular bed suitable.

edit.old: | **Staged BMG** | Allows graft maturation; applicable when all local tissue compromised | Two operations; prolonged SPC; no female-specific data; ~ 19% stage-1 revision (male data) | Obliterative stricture with no viable local tissue |
edit.new: | **Staged BMG** | Permits assessment of an open graft plate before closure when a viable bed is available | May require graft revision; drainage and continence outcomes are unreported in women; stage-1 revision occurred in 17/91 men in one series | Selected complex defects with a viable graft bed when single-stage repair is unsuitable |

finding: The 90% outcome row can be read as success after tubularized reconstruction in 91 men. Only 51/91 underwent stage 2; 17 were awaiting it and 23 planned no closure, while 9/91 needed scheduled dilation or chronic catheter.
evidence: PMID 23876581, DOI 10.1016/j.urology.2013.03.081, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23876581/ — Kozinn et al. report 91 enrolled, 51 tubularized, 17 pending closure, 23 stage 1 only, mean follow-up 15 months, and 9/91 reconstruction failures by scheduled dilation or chronic catheter.

edit.new: | Kozinn 2013<sup>[[6]](#ref6)</sup> | Male, complex | Multistage BMG | 91 enrolled; 51 tubularized | 82/91 (90%) avoided scheduled dilation or chronic catheter; this is not stage-2-specific success | Mean 15 mo (whole cohort) |

finding: Prolonged suprapubic catheter dependence is described as inherent to a planned staged repair. In the male template, patients can void through a proximal urethrostomy or open plate between stages, so female drainage must be planned for the actual anatomy.
evidence: EAU Urethral Strictures Guideline 2026, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urethral-strictures/chapter/perioperative-care-of-urethral-surgery — §10.3 says the catheter can be removed 3–5 days after first-stage urethroplasty; Mori and Angermeier, PMID 26816806, https://tau.amegroups.org/article/view/5678/html describe voiding after first-stage proximal urethrostomy.

edit.old: - **Two operations**, with prolonged SPC dependence between stages (several months in male series).
edit.new: - **Planned second operation** after graft maturation. Urinary drainage between stages depends on anatomy and repair; prolonged suprapubic catheter use is not inherent to the male staged template.

finding: The page repeats a percentage error printed in the Palminteri abstract: 23/24 equals 95.8%, not 92.8%. Correct both page occurrences while preserving the published n/N and noting the source discrepancy.
evidence: PMID 11743290, DOI 10.1016/S0022-5347(05)65397-9, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11743290/ — the abstract reports 23 of 24 men without recurrent stricture at median 18 months but prints 92.8%; arithmetic gives 95.8%.

finding: The Outcomes section reports patency but gives no follow-up decision point for recurrence, continence or fistula after reconstruction. A general urethroplasty follow-up recommendation can be stated without inventing a female staged-BMG protocol.
evidence: EAU Urethral Strictures Guideline 2026, https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urethral-strictures/chapter/followup — §11.6 gives a Strong recommendation for at least one year of follow-up and separates anatomic from patient-reported outcomes; https://uroweb.org/guidelines/urethral-strictures/chapter/disease-management-in-females — §7.3.2 reports new incontinence after female BMG repair.

edit.old: There are no published female-specific series reporting outcomes of staged BMG urethroplasty as a distinct technique.
edit.new: There are no published female-specific series reporting outcomes of staged BMG urethroplasty as a distinct technique. After reconstruction, assess recurrent obstruction, continence, fistula and patient-reported voiding. The EAU 2026 guideline strongly recommends at least one year of follow-up after urethroplasty but gives no female staged-BMG schedule.
